data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=27, so the reservoir averages \boxed{27\text{ ft}}.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=27+4=31\text{ ft}\qquad \text{minimum}=27-4=23\text{ ft}

the reservoir is highest in July at 31\text{ ft} and lowest in January at 23\text{ ft}, so the range of levels is \boxed{[23\text{ ft},\ 31\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} @index_unit@, and so the level follows a yearly cycle and repeats every 12 months.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-4)=0 \implies x-4=0 \implies x=4

The phase shift is \boxed{4} months, and so the pattern is shifted 4 months to the right: the level is at its average and rising in April, peaks in July, and is lowest in January.

Part (e). Substitute x=5 (May):

data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=30, so the reservoir averages \boxed{30\text{ ft}}.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=30+6=36\text{ ft}\qquad \text{minimum}=30-6=24\text{ ft}

the reservoir is highest in May at 36\text{ ft} and lowest in November at 24\text{ ft}, so the range of levels is \boxed{[24\text{ ft},\ 36\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

data.solution_steps:

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=25+4=29\text{ ft}\qquad \text{minimum}=25-4=21\text{ ft}

the reservoir is highest in May at 29\text{ ft} and lowest in November at 21\text{ ft}, so the range of levels is \boxed{[21\text{ ft},\ 29\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-2)=0 \implies x-2=0 \implies x=2

data.part_b: What are the highest and lowest water levels of the reservoir?

data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the water level in October. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=18, so the reservoir averages \boxed{18\text{ ft}}.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=18+6=24\text{ ft}\qquad \text{minimum}=18-6=12\text{ ft}

the reservoir is highest in August at 24\text{ ft} and lowest in February at 12\text{ ft}, so the range of levels is \boxed{[12\text{ ft},\ 24\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} @index_unit@, and so the level follows a yearly cycle and repeats every 12 months.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-5)=0 \implies x-5=0 \implies x=5

The phase shift is \boxed{5} months, and so the pattern is shifted 5 months to the right: the level is at its average and rising in May, peaks in August, and is lowest in February.

Part (e). Substitute x=10 (October):

L(10)=6\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(10-5)\right]+18=6\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+18=24\text{ ft}

So the model predicts a water level of about \boxed{24.0\text{ ft}} in October.

data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=27, so the reservoir averages \boxed{27\text{ ft}}.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=27+8=35\text{ ft}\qquad \text{minimum}=27-8=19\text{ ft}

\text{maximum}=26+6=32\text{ ft}\qquad \text{minimum}=26-6=20\text{ ft}
